Hap
HAP
n. (chance; fortune; that which happens without apparent design; luck)
Old Norse happ, chance, good luck. The word is the ancestor of happen, happy, and perhaps, though it stands alone in the Authorized Version as a single bare noun, naming the raw fact of an unplanned occurrence.

Biblical Definition

Ruth's second chapter turns on this one small word at the exact moment the whole book pivots. Ruth, a Moabite widow gleaning to keep herself and Naomi alive, asks no favor and follows no plan beyond the ordinary law of gleaning; the text is careful to record that her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech. Nothing in the sentence claims Ruth aimed herself at that field, or that Boaz had summoned her there. By every visible measure it was chance, hap, an unplanned landing in one field among many she might have entered.

The rest of the book is Scripture's own commentary on that hap. Naomi, hearing where Ruth had gleaned, immediately recognizes what neither Ruth nor the narrative voice has yet said aloud — the man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen — and the whole redemption plot that follows, ending in the birth of Obed, the grandfather of David, unfolds from that one bare hap. The word is never explained away or spiritualized into a hidden miracle; it is left standing exactly as hap, an ordinary chance landing, and the book's quiet argument is that the LORD's providence works precisely through such unremarkable, undirected, entirely ordinary happenings, needing no more visible hand than a tired widow choosing one field over another.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): chance; fortune; that which happens or comes to pass without design; luck; hazard.

expand to see more

HAP, n. That which happens or falls out; chance; fortune; luck; an event without apparent design.

GLEAN, v.i. To gather stalks or ears of grain left by reapers, as permitted to the poor under Mosaic law.

KINSMAN, n. A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.

REDEEM, v.t. To buy back; to repurchase; to ransom; to recover a right or possession by payment or exchange.

PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; divine direction or superintendence.

Key Scripture

Rut 2:2 — "And Ruth the Moabitess said unto Naomi, Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn after him in whose sight I shall find grace. And she said unto her, Go, my daughter."

Rut 2:3 — "And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech."

Rut 2:20 — "And Naomi said unto her daughter in law, Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead. And Naomi said unto her, The man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen."

Pro 16:33 — "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Hap is treated as proof that no hand governs an outcome, when Ruth's whole plot is built to show that an event genuinely undirected by any visible human plan can still be entirely governed by the LORD's providence.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; hap still names an unplanned occurrence. The principle worth recovering is how carefully the book of Ruth holds chance and providence together as one event seen at two heights, rather than erasing either to make the story simpler. Ruth's landing in Boaz's field really was hap, by every measure available to the people living through it; the text does not pretend she or anyone else steered it there.

Proverbs states the doctrine the narrative of Ruth only shows: the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD. A hap and a providence are not, in Scripture's own accounting, rival explanations competing for the same event — they are two true descriptions of the same event, seen from two different heights. What looked, from the ground, like an ordinary widow choosing one field among many looked, from the vantage the book itself supplies, like the exact hinge on which the ancestry of David and, in time, of Christ, would turn.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew miqreh (H4745), a happening, a chance occurrence; the noun behind “hap” in Ruth 2:3, from the verb qarah, to meet or befall.

expand to see more

Hebrew miqreh (H4745) — a happening, a chance, an accident; the noun rendered “hap” in Ruth 2:3.

Hebrew qarah (H7136) — to happen, to befall, to meet; the verb root behind miqreh, used of ordinary encounters throughout the Old Testament.

Hebrew laqat (H3950) — to glean, to gather up; Ruth's own activity at the moment her hap occurred.

Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; the office Boaz will come to fill because of this hap.

Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot; the object cast in Proverbs 16:33, the standing Old Testament figure for a matter left, on the surface, to chance.

Usage

"“her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz” — the small, unplanned turn on which the book of Ruth pivots."

"“the man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen” — Naomi's recognition of what the hap had actually delivered."

"“the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” — the doctrine underneath every such hap."
